lyrics:
Wazoo? He thinks the room is beneath him
Counts every ticket, then insults the seats
Technique, certainly. Feeling? I doubt it
Everything measured; nothing that bleeds
Smarter than everyone. That's the posture
Filth when the difficult music runs long
Calls it satire whenever you catch him
Ask what he loves. He'll tell you what's wrong

So what do we call it
Contempt? Vanity
Cruelty dressed up
as integrity
You made the impression
You fed us the evidence
What else are we meant to believe

I wrote what I heard
I said what I saw
You wanted approval
I wouldn't applaud
Call that contempt
Call honesty ugly
Wazoo in effigy
Guilty

Pretentious, academic — put that in print
Difficult mostly for difficulty's sake
A talent for sneering, a taste for the gutter
He calls it a mirror. I call it a fake
And can he play rock? Well, hardly the question
A loser in costume, impressed with his brain
You'll find this opinion remarkably common
Ask anyone qualified. Ask them again

So what do we call it
Contempt? Vanity
Cruelty dressed up
as integrity
You made the impression
You handed us kindling
What else were we given to hear

I wrote what I heard
I said what I saw
You wanted approval
I wouldn't applaud
Call that contempt
Call honesty ugly
Wazoo in effigy
Guilty

Ask the men who were in the band beside him
Ask what perfection was worth in the end
Three hundred dollars to make both the records
Ten thousand later for hired-in men
A phone call finished what years had assembled
The salaries stopped. As of last week. That's clear
Brilliant, perhaps — but brilliance is cheaper
When somebody else pays the price to be near

So I asked the wild side hero
"Wazoo? The single most untalented person I've heard in my life
Two-bit
Pretentious
Academic
He can't play his way out of anything."
Twenty years later, that same wild man
Stood at a podium and inducted him into the Hall
No correction was printed
Corrections are not printed

By then he was dying. He went there regardless
Germany. Conducting. That unplayable score
They played it. The room stayed on its feet twenty minutes
Sentiment, surely. We've seen it before
No need to revise what was already printed
No reason to soften a judgment because —

Like I invented this

I wrote what I heard

Have I got to listen to this
Talentless

review.review_text:
“Wazoo in Effigy” closes the record by putting its subject on trial, though the verdict was apparently reached long before the first note. Rose builds the song almost entirely from accusation: arrogant, academic, vulgar, cruel, pretentious, emotionally sterile, impossible to work for. The clipped baritone of the verses doesn’t defend Wazoo; it reads the charges with the confidence of people who have repeated them often enough to stop examining them.

That distinction matters, because the chorus belongs to another voice. “I wrote what I heard. / I said what I saw. / You wanted approval; / I wouldn’t applaud.” It isn’t an acquittal and barely qualifies as a defense. Wazoo accepts the evidence and rejects the interpretation. When the question finally comes — “Wazoo in effigy?” — the answer is simply “Guilty.”

Musically, Rose gives the argument an appropriately unstable frame. Marimba figures, brass blocks, woodwind counterpoint and abrupt metric shifts continually reorganize themselves beneath a vocal that refuses to become excited. The arrangement grows increasingly elaborate while the singer grows increasingly matter-of-fact, a reversal that keeps the song from becoming either tribute or courtroom melodrama.

The strongest section arrives when the song stops arguing altogether. A “wild side hero” dismisses Wazoo as talentless, pretentious and academic; decades later he stands at a podium to induct the same man into the Hall. “No correction was printed. / Corrections are not printed.” Rose wisely leaves the contradiction sitting there. The following image of a dying composer traveling to Germany to conduct supposedly unplayable music pushes the point further without turning it into vindication.

Then comes the smallest and perhaps most revealing line in the song: “Like I invented this?” For the first time Wazoo sounds less like a defendant than a man baffled that being himself has somehow become another charge against him.

The final “Talentless” is therefore not Rose delivering a verdict on Frank Zappa. It is the old verdict surviving after the evidence around it has changed.

That makes “Wazoo in Effigy” an unusually appropriate closer: funny in places, hostile in others, technically obsessive, stubbornly unresolved, and unwilling to tell the listener whom to believe. The effigy burns. The work remains.
